title: The World Is Running Out of Oil Reserves. India Cannot Afford to Wait.
excerpt: The EIA warned that OECD oil inventories are headed to their lowest levels since 2003. India, which imports 85% of its crude, faces an existential squeeze.
body:
The world's oil cupboard is nearly bare, and India — which imports 85% of its crude — is running out of time.

The US Energy Information Administration warned on Tuesday that oil inventories across OECD nations are plunging toward their lowest levels since at least 2003. Total stockpiles will fall to just under 2.3 billion barrels by December, the EIA projected, as consuming nations burn through reserves at a record pace to replace the 11 million barrels per day of Middle Eastern output lost to the Iran war.

The numbers are staggering. Global crude and fuel stocks fell at a pace of 5.27 million barrels per day in March, accelerated to 8.62 million in April, and likely approached 9 million in May. June could see draws of 11 million barrels per day as summer demand kicks in — the equivalent of running down Saudi Arabia's entire pre-war production every single day.

## The "Tank Bottoms" Warning

Oil industry executives have started using a term that makes traders nervous: tank bottoms. It refers to the point at which commercial storage runs so low that the system can no longer function as a market buffer — when pipelines, refineries, and tanker fleets cannot keep product moving smoothly.

"We're approaching unheard of inventory levels," a senior ExxonMobil executive told investors at a recent conference.

The math is unforgiving. Global commercial inventories stood at roughly 8.5 billion barrels when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz on February 28. But the operational minimum — the floor below which the system seizes up — is approximately 6.8 billion barrels. That means the actual usable buffer was never 8.5 billion. It was 1.7 billion.

At current drawdown rates, the world reaches "operational stress" this month. A bidding war for scarce barrels could begin by September.

## India's Exposure

No major economy is more exposed than India. The country consumes roughly 5.5 million barrels per day, and its dependence on imports has only deepened as domestic production stagnates.

India's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53% in April from March. Benchmark Brent crude, which traded below $70 before the war, hovered around $92 on Tuesday — down 2% after Iran and Israel announced a halt to direct attacks, but still 30% above pre-conflict levels.

The Reserve Bank of India last Friday unveiled emergency measures — concessional forex swap facilities for banks' overseas borrowings, capital gains tax exemptions on government bonds, and expanded access for foreign investors — that Jefferies estimates could pull in $50 billion to $70 billion in capital inflows. The rupee gained 0.4% on Tuesday to 95.35 per dollar.

But those measures address the symptoms, not the cause. India cannot print oil.

## Demand Destruction Has Already Begun

The EIA made a striking admission in Tuesday's report: it now expects global oil demand to shrink in 2026, reversing its earlier forecast of a rise. This would be the first demand decline since the pandemic year of 2020 — and it is not voluntary. It reflects forced conservation, government-mandated consumption cuts, and the simple reality that oil at $90-plus a barrel is pricing out the most vulnerable consumers.

India has already taken steps that would have been unthinkable a year ago. The government is urging citizens to limit foreign travel, pushing for greater use of public transport, and curbing gold imports. Meanwhile, HSBC forecasts India's balance of payments deficit could swell to $65 billion in 2026-27 before the RBI's new measures shave off roughly $30 billion.

## The Strait Stays Shut

The core problem is simple: the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. The EIA's projections assume marine traffic through the strait won't return to pre-conflict levels until early 2027 — a timeline that would push global inventories into genuinely uncharted territory.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that even if a peace deal materialises, roughly 500 million barrels of crude and refined products would need to clear the strait just to replenish what has been consumed. At a surplus of one million barrels per day, restocking alone would take more than a year.

Prediction markets assign an 11% chance that Hormuz reopens by the end of June. For India, the arithmetic is existential: every day the strait stays closed, the country burns through reserves it cannot easily replace, at prices it cannot easily afford, in a market that is running out of room to absorb the shock.
